entities.summary:
The Secret Army Organization (OAS), a clandestine paramilitary group, emerged in France during the Algerian War of Independence (1954-1962) and played a pivotal role in shaping contemporary French political discourse. Founded in 1961 by former members of the French military and right-wing activists, it sought to maintain French Algeria through violent means, reflecting the tensions between colonial loyalty and rising independence movements. The OAS is significant as it embodies the extreme nationalist sentiments that persisted in France following the loss of Algeria in 1962, influencing both political extremism and the discourse on immigration and national identity in France.

The OAS engaged in a series of violent acts, including bombings and assassinations, targeting both Algerian nationalists and French officials who supported Algerian independence. Notably, the assassination attempt on President Charles de Gaulle in 1962 underscored their desperation and the radicalization of some factions within the French right. Despite its efforts, the organization was unable to prevent the decolonization process and was officially dissolved in 1963 after a crackdown by French authorities. The group’s activities highlighted the violent resistance to decolonization, and its legacy continues to resonate in discussions regarding French nationalism and the challenges of integrating former colonial subjects into French society.
